What’s up with the strange animals on programming books?

If you’ve worked with programmers, you’ve seen the O’Reilly manuals on topics as arcane as Prompt Engineering, Software Architecture, Kafka and Rust. They grew out of Tim O’Reilly’s education and consulting business.

Tim started in the early 80s selling how-to manuals for software. He worked with the alpha-geeks and translated their knowledge for everyone else, and by the late 90s he was running conferences for tech’s executives and engineers. Today O’Reilly Media is a huge business, and Tim turned that authority into a second career as a venture capitalist.

The cheeky animals had a lot to do with it.

In the mid-80s, the Nutshell Handbooks were sold by mail order in plain brown covers held together with staples. When Tim wanted them in bookstores, they needed real covers. He didn’t like the first designer’s attempt, so Edie Freedman, a staffer’s neighbor, took a look.

She’d never used Unix or met a Unix programmer. But words like vi, sed, awk, lex, yacc and curses sounded like Dungeons & Dragons to her, so she went looking for images just as strange: 19th-century animal engravings from the Dover Pictorial Archive. When she found a pair of slender lorises, she knew they were sed and awk.

The staff thought they were weird, ugly and scary. Tim got it instantly: the quirk would make the books impossible to miss on a shelf.

Great branding plus a place inside a new community is the perfect recipe for a media brand.

P.S. Tim is part of what Stanford historian Fred Turner calls “network celebrity.” To see how he connects to the father of cybernetics and the godfather of California counterculture, follow along!

How does a page wrap text around a moving disc, 60 times a second, without asking the browser where each line ends?

The answer is Pretext, by Cheng Lou (who worked on React and Midjourney): a TypeScript library that measures and breaks text without touching the DOM. You call prepare(text, font) once, then layout(prepared, maxWidth, lineHeight), which is plain arithmetic.

The trick: measure every word once with the canvas and keep the widths. A line break is just addition. In the video, "Your CSS can't do this. But this library can." at 500 px adds up to 457.12 px at "this."; "But" (72.64 px) would make it 544.41, past 500, so the line breaks. Around the disc (radius 220 px), a line whose text sits 184 px from the center meets a chord of 2·√(220² − 184²) = 241.2 px, which leaves 317.4 px on each side.

The cost: resizing 1,000 posts by reading their heights one by one takes the DOM 476 ms per width, about 28.6 frames at 60 fps. Pretext's layout() takes 0.245 ms.

476 ms ÷ 0.245 ms ≈ 1,944× faster (the full run, 40 widths, gives 19,460 ms ÷ 10.0 ms = 1,944×). The one-time prepare() of the 1,000 posts is 54.6 ms. Heights match the DOM in 39,988 of 40,000 cases.

Measured here on a notebook (i5-1235U, Chromium 145). Code: github.com/chenglou/pretext, MIT, 50,843 stars (GitHub API, Oct 20, 2026).

Would you swap getBoundingClientRect for this?
